issues.legal_issue: A person who possesses and uses a building in its own right may claim business depreciation even without formal legal title where it has acquired beneficial dominion over the building.
material_facts: The company was allotted seven houses after making part payments toward their purchase, and possession was delivered to it although no conveyance deed had been executed.
The company exercised dominion over the houses, allotted them to its staff, and the staff used them for the company's business purposes.
The tax authorities denied depreciation because the company lacked a registered conveyance deed; the Supreme Court reviewed that denial on appeal.
issues.conclusion: The company was entitled to claim depreciation. The appeal was allowed, the High Court's judgment was set aside, and the referred question was answered against the Revenue and in favour of the company.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 32(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, “owned” is interpreted contextually and broadly: a person who has acquired possession in its own right, exercises dominion that excludes others, and uses the building for its business may be treated as its owner for depreciation even without a formal conveyance. The Court relied on CIT v. Podar Cement Pvt. Ltd. (1997), which adopted a contextual approach to ownership under section 22; R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala v. CIT (1971), concerning a person able to exercise ownership rights in their own right; State of U.P. v. Renusagar Power Company (1991), on the broad meaning of “own”; Perry v. Clissold, quoted with approval in Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K. C. Alexander (1968), on possessory title; and Badiani P. K. v. CIT (1976), on depreciation as an allowance reflecting loss in asset value. The Court distinguished the ordinary legal requirements for transferring immovable property, including those under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and the Registration Act, from the contextual meaning of ownership for this tax benefit. It also applied the principle that an ambiguous taxing provision should be interpreted in the way favourable to the assessee.

rule.if: business_asset_depreciation_claim and actual_business_use and (legal_title_conveyed or (allotted_for_acquisition and part_payment_toward_acquisition and possession_delivered and dominion_in_own_right and exclusion_right))

predicates.business_asset_depreciation_claim: The claimant seeks depreciation on a building or other asset used for its business or profession.
predicates.actual_business_use: The claimant actually uses the asset for its business or profession.
predicates.legal_title_conveyed: Legal title to the asset has been conveyed to the claimant.
predicates.allotted_for_acquisition: The asset has been allotted to the claimant as part of an arrangement to acquire it.
predicates.part_payment_toward_acquisition: The claimant has made part payment toward acquiring the asset.
predicates.possession_delivered: The claimant has been given possession of the asset.
predicates.dominion_in_own_right: The claimant exercises dominion over the asset in its own right.
predicates.exclusion_right: The claimant is entitled to exclude others from the asset.

issues.definition: When a business depreciation claim concerns an asset actually used for business, depreciation is allowable if the claimant has legal title or has been allotted the asset for acquisition, made part payment, received possession, and exercises dominion with the right to exclude others.
